response.passage: Consumer exploitation occurs across all segments of society, regardless of a person's education level or financial status, as even well-informed individuals can be misled by deceptive advertising or hidden product defects. Many consumers mistakenly believe that purchasing from high-end, branded retail outlets guarantees absolute purity, yet even premium stores can unknowingly sell adulterated or substandard goods. To protect the public, the government has established specific certification marks that act as quality indicators. For instance, the ISI mark is mandatory for industrial and electrical products to ensure safety, while the Agmark is specifically designated for agricultural and food-related items. When a consumer faces exploitation, they do not need to approach the highest judicial body immediately. Instead, the Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) provides a three-tier quasi-judicial machinery. Consumers can file complaints at the District, State, or National level depending on the value of the goods or services involved. This tiered system ensures that justice is accessible and affordable for everyone, preventing the need for expensive litigation in the Supreme Court for minor grievances. By understanding these rights and the purpose of various certification marks, consumers can make informed choices and seek appropriate redressal for any unfair trade practices they encounter in the market.
response.summary: Consumer exploitation affects everyone, so it is important to understand that brands do not guarantee safety and specific marks like ISI or Agmark are used for quality. The Consumer Protection Act provides a tiered court system to resolve disputes locally rather than going to the Supreme Court.
